title: Bird song dialects
text: Biologists long assumed that the songs of a given bird species were fixed by its genes, so that a sparrow raised in isolation would sing exactly as its wild relatives do. Experiments in which nestlings were reared without adult tutors overturned this view. The isolated birds produced songs with the basic rhythm of their species but lacking the local flourishes that distinguish one population from another. These regional variants, it turned out, are learned during a brief sensitive period early in life, much as human children absorb the accent of the place where they grow up.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: describe how evidence revised an earlier belief about the origins of bird song
argue that bird song is entirely learned rather than inherited
compare the learning abilities of birds and human children
explain why some bird populations sing more complex songs than others
criticize the methods used in early studies of bird song
questions.explanation: The passage presents the old view (songs fixed by genes), then the experiments that overturned it. It does not say song is *entirely* learned: the isolated birds kept the basic rhythm.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about a sparrow raised in isolation? Select all that apply.
choices: Its song would show the basic rhythm typical of its species.
Its song would lack features specific to a local population.
It would be unable to produce any song at all.
questions.explanation: The isolated birds had the species' basic rhythm but lacked the local flourishes. The passage says they did produce songs, so the third choice is false.

title: The printing press and error
text: It is often said that printing made texts more reliable than hand copying, since every copy of an edition was identical. Yet identity cuts both ways. A scribe's slip affected one manuscript; a compositor's slip was reproduced in every copy of a print run, sometimes hundreds at once. Early printers knew this and often corrected errors while the press was running, so that copies of the same edition can differ in small ways. The reliability of print, in other words, was not given by the technology itself but achieved through practices that grew up around it.

questions.stem: The author mentions the corrections made while the press was running in order to
choices: show that copies of a printed edition were not always identical
prove that scribes made more errors than compositors
suggest that early printers were careless
argue that hand copying was more reliable than printing
explain why print runs were limited to a few hundred copies
questions.explanation: Right after mentioning the corrections, the author says copies of the same edition can differ, which qualifies the claim that every copy was identical.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the common claim in the first sentence is best described as
choices: qualified skepticism
complete agreement
open hostility
amused indifference
reluctant admiration
questions.explanation: The author does not reject the claim outright but complicates it: reliability was achieved, not automatic. That is qualified skepticism.

title: Urban heat islands
text:
Cities are, on average, several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island. The causes are well understood. Asphalt and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat at night; buildings block the wind that would otherwise carry warm air away; and air conditioners, vehicles and factories add heat directly. The effect is strongest on calm, clear nights, when rural land cools quickly but the city's stored heat keeps temperatures high.

Mitigation strategies follow from these causes. Light-colored roofs and pavements reflect more sunlight and store less heat. Trees shade surfaces and cool the air as water evaporates from their leaves. Some cities have begun to require reflective roofing on new buildings, and others have launched planting programs aimed at neighborhoods with little shade.

These measures are not equally effective everywhere, however. In humid climates, the cooling from evaporation is weaker, because air that is already moist absorbs less water vapor. And reflective surfaces at street level can bounce sunlight onto pedestrians and nearby walls, raising the temperatures people actually feel even as surface temperatures fall. Planners have therefore come to see heat mitigation less as a matter of adopting a single best technology than of fitting a mix of measures to local conditions.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the urban heat island effect is most pronounced
choices: on calm, clear nights
on hot, windy afternoons
during periods of heavy rain
in cities with many trees
in the early morning in winter
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the effect is strongest on calm, clear nights, when rural land cools fast but the city keeps its stored heat.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that tree planting would be least effective at cooling a city that
choices: has a humid climate
has many reflective roofs
is located in a desert
has few factories
has wide streets
questions.explanation: Trees cool partly by evaporation, and the third paragraph says evaporative cooling is weaker in humid climates.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the passage present as a possible drawback of a heat mitigation measure? Select all that apply.
choices: Reflective pavement can raise the temperature that pedestrians feel.
Evaporative cooling works less well when the air is already moist.
Light-colored roofs are more expensive than dark ones.
questions.explanation: Both of the first two are in the final paragraph. Cost is never mentioned.

questions.stem: Which sentence in the passage states the conclusion that planners have drawn?
choices: Planners have therefore come to see heat mitigation less as a matter of adopting a single best technology than of fitting a mix of measures to local conditions.
Mitigation strategies follow from these causes.
Some cities have begun to require reflective roofing on new buildings, and others have launched planting programs aimed at neighborhoods with little shade.
The causes are well understood.
questions.explanation: *Therefore* marks the last sentence as the conclusion planners drew from the limits just described.

title: Reading the ledger
text: Historians of everyday life have learned to read account books as more than lists of numbers. A shopkeeper's ledger records not only what was sold but to whom, on what terms and how often debts went unpaid. From such entries one can reconstruct networks of credit and trust that no diary describes, since those who kept the books rarely thought their routine dealings worth writing about elsewhere.

questions.stem: The passage implies that ledgers are valuable to historians partly because
choices: they record information that the people involved seldom wrote down in other forms
they are more accurate than diaries about prices
shopkeepers wrote detailed accounts of their customers' lives
they were kept by every household
they describe political events in detail
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the bookkeepers rarely wrote about routine dealings elsewhere, so ledgers capture what no diary describes.

title: The puzzle of cooperation
text:
Why do animals help one another when helping has a cost? For decades the leading answer was kin selection: an animal that aids its relatives promotes copies of its own genes, so helping can spread even when it harms the helper. Kin selection explains a great deal, from worker bees that never reproduce to ground squirrels that risk their lives to warn relatives of predators.

But not all cooperation is among kin. Vampire bats that have fed share blood with roostmates that have not, including unrelated ones, and a bat that has received blood is more likely to give it later to the bat that fed it. Such reciprocal exchange can be stable as long as animals interact repeatedly and can recognize, and refuse to help, those who take without giving back.

The two explanations are not rivals so much as tools for different cases. Where relatives live together, kin selection may dominate; where unrelated individuals meet again and again, reciprocity can do the work. Many animal societies probably rely on both.

questions.stem: The author mentions ground squirrels primarily as an example of
choices: behavior that kin selection can explain
cooperation among unrelated animals
reciprocal exchange
an animal that refuses to help cheaters
a species that does not cooperate
questions.explanation: Ground squirrels warning relatives are listed among the things kin selection explains.

questions.stem: According to the passage, reciprocal exchange can remain stable only if animals
choices: meet repeatedly and can identify individuals who do not return help
are closely related to one another
live in very large groups
share food every day
never compete for resources
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names two conditions: repeated interaction, and recognizing and refusing those who take without giving.

questions.stem: The final paragraph serves mainly to
choices: reconcile the two explanations by assigning each to the situations it fits
reject kin selection in favor of reciprocity
argue that neither explanation is supported by evidence
introduce a third explanation of cooperation
summarize the evidence from vampire bats
questions.explanation: *Not rivals so much as tools for different cases*: the paragraph says each explanation fits different conditions and both may operate.

title: Translation and loss
text: Discussions of literary translation tend to dwell on what is lost: the pun that cannot survive the move to another language, the rhythm that collapses, the allusion no foreign reader will catch. Less often noticed is what translation can add. A translator forced to find an equivalent for an untranslatable phrase sometimes produces an image the original lacked, and readers of the translation may encounter a work that is different from, but not simply poorer than, its source.

questions.stem: The author's main point is that
choices: translation can create new qualities as well as lose existing ones
most translations are poorer than their originals
puns are the hardest element of a text to translate
readers should learn foreign languages rather than read translations
translators should avoid adding images to a text
questions.explanation: After noting the usual focus on loss, the author stresses what translation can add, so the work becomes different but not simply poorer.

questions.stem: The phrase "different from, but not simply poorer than" serves to
choices: reject the assumption that a translation is merely a diminished version of the original
claim that translations are better than originals
argue that translations should be judged by the same standards as originals
concede that translations always lose some meaning
express doubt about the value of translation
questions.explanation: *Not simply poorer* pushes back against the loss-only view: the translation is not just the original minus something.

title: Monetary policy and expectations
text:
Central banks once operated in secrecy, on the theory that surprise made policy more powerful. If firms and workers did not know that interest rates were about to fall, the reasoning went, a cut would jolt spending more than an expected one. Over the past few decades, this view has largely been reversed. Most central banks now announce their targets, publish their forecasts and explain their decisions at length.

The change reflects a new understanding of how policy works. Much of the effect of a rate decision comes not from the decision itself but from what it signals about future policy. Long-term borrowing costs, which matter most for mortgages and business investment, depend on expectations of short-term rates years ahead. A central bank that communicates clearly can therefore move long-term rates without changing short-term rates at all, simply by changing what people expect it to do.

Clarity has its own risks. A bank that commits too firmly to a future path may find it hard to change course when conditions shift without damaging its credibility. The art of communication lies in guiding expectations while preserving room to adapt.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the older practice of secrecy rested on the belief that
choices: unexpected policy changes have a larger effect on spending
clear communication reduces a central bank's credibility
long-term rates depend on expectations
firms ignore interest rate decisions
publishing forecasts would cause inflation
questions.explanation: The first paragraph: surprise made policy more powerful, since an unexpected cut would jolt spending more.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that a central bank could lower long-term borrowing costs by
choices: persuading people that short-term rates will stay low for years
raising short-term rates sharply
keeping its forecasts secret
refusing to explain its decisions
committing to change policy frequently
questions.explanation: Long-term rates depend on expected future short-term rates, so convincing people that short-term rates will stay low pulls long-term rates down.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the passage present as true of central bank communication today? Select all that apply.
choices: It can influence long-term rates without a change in short-term rates.
It carries the risk of limiting a bank's flexibility.
It has replaced interest rate decisions as the main tool of policy.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph supports the first choice and the third paragraph the second. The passage never says communication has replaced rate decisions.

title: Dating ancient fires
text: Charcoal found in an ancient hearth can be dated by measuring its radioactive carbon, but the date tells us when the wood stopped growing, not when it was burned. If the people who built the fire used old driftwood or the inner rings of a long-lived tree, the charcoal may be centuries older than the fire itself. Archaeologists therefore prefer to date the remains of short-lived materials, such as seeds or twigs, found in the same layer.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that dating seeds rather than charcoal is preferred because seeds
choices: are likely to have formed close to the time of the fire
contain more radioactive carbon than wood
are found more often in hearths
burn more completely than wood
were never used as fuel
questions.explanation: Short-lived materials stopped growing shortly before they were deposited, so their date is close to the fire's. Old wood can be centuries older.

title: The rise of the essay
text:
The essay as a form owes its name and much of its character to Michel de Montaigne, who in the 1570s began writing short pieces he called essais, or attempts. The word captures what was new about them. Montaigne did not set out to prove a thesis or instruct a reader; he tried out ideas, followed digressions and contradicted himself without apology. His subject, he said, was himself, and his self was changeable.

Later writers in English kept the name but often changed the spirit. Francis Bacon's essays, published at the end of the same century, are compact and authoritative, closer to collections of maxims than to Montaigne's meandering explorations. The tension between these two models, the essay as exploration and the essay as pronouncement, runs through the history of the form.

Modern readers sometimes treat the five-paragraph school essay as the essay's natural shape. Montaigne would hardly have recognized it. Its fixed structure of thesis, three supporting points and conclusion belongs to Bacon's line, and arguably exaggerates even that.

questions.stem: The author discusses the meaning of the word essais in order to
choices: highlight the exploratory character of Montaigne's writing
show that Montaigne wrote in French
argue that Bacon misunderstood Montaigne
explain why essays are short
criticize Montaigne's lack of structure
questions.explanation: *The word captures what was new about them*: essais means attempts, matching Montaigne's habit of trying out ideas.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that the five-paragraph school essay
choices: is closer in spirit to Bacon's essays than to Montaigne's
is the natural form of the essay
was invented by Montaigne
combines the best features of both traditions
has no connection to earlier essay writing
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says its fixed structure belongs to Bacon's line.

questions.stem: In the context of the passage, "pronouncement" most nearly means
choices: authoritative statement
pronunciation
public announcement of an event
legal judgment
formal greeting
questions.explanation: It is contrasted with exploration and refers to Bacon's compact, authoritative style, so it means an authoritative statement.

title: Placebos without deception
text: Placebos are usually thought to work only when patients believe they are receiving real treatment. Several recent trials, however, have given patients pills openly described as inert and still found modest improvements in symptoms such as pain and fatigue. Researchers caution that these effects are smaller than those of many active drugs and appear mostly in conditions where symptoms depend heavily on attention and expectation. Still, the results challenge the assumption that deception is essential to the placebo effect.

questions.stem: The trials described in the passage are significant mainly because they
choices: call into question the belief that placebos require patients to be deceived
show that placebos are as effective as active drugs
prove that pain is caused by expectation
demonstrate that placebos work for all conditions
reveal that patients often know when they receive a placebo
questions.explanation: The final sentence says the results challenge the assumption that deception is essential. The passage notes the effects were modest and limited, so the other claims overreach.

questions.stem: The researchers' caution, as described in the passage, includes which of the following points? Select all that apply.
choices: The improvements were smaller than those of many active drugs.
The effects appeared mainly in conditions tied to attention and expectation.
The patients had secretly been given active drugs.
questions.explanation: Both of the first two are stated. Nothing suggests the pills were secretly active.

title: Glaciers as archives
text:
Ice that accumulates on a glacier year after year traps tiny bubbles of air, and those bubbles preserve samples of the atmosphere at the time the snow fell. By drilling cores from the thickest ice sheets and analyzing the air in successive layers, scientists have reconstructed carbon dioxide levels stretching back hundreds of thousands of years.

The method has a subtlety that is easy to overlook. Snow does not seal off its air at once; it is slowly compressed into firn, a granular material through which air continues to circulate, and only becomes solid ice tens of meters down. The trapped air is therefore younger than the ice around it, sometimes by thousands of years. Researchers must estimate this age gap and correct for it before comparing carbon dioxide records with temperature records drawn from the ice itself.

When such corrections are made carefully, the records show carbon dioxide and temperature rising and falling together through successive ice ages, a pattern that has become one of the strongest pieces of evidence for the link between the two.

questions.stem: According to the passage, air trapped in ice is younger than the surrounding ice because
choices: air continues to circulate through firn until it becomes solid ice
bubbles rise through the ice over time
scientists contaminate samples during drilling
carbon dioxide breaks down in ice
snow falls more slowly in cold years
questions.explanation: The second paragraph: air keeps circulating through firn until tens of meters down, so it is sealed later than the snow fell.

questions.stem: The author mentions the need to "correct for" the age gap in order to
choices: explain a step needed before carbon dioxide and temperature records can be compared
suggest that ice core records are unreliable
argue that temperature records are more accurate than carbon dioxide records
show that firn is a recent discovery
criticize earlier researchers
questions.explanation: The correction is required *before comparing carbon dioxide records with temperature records*.

questions.stem: Which sentence in the passage presents the main finding that the method has supported?
choices: When such corrections are made carefully, the records show carbon dioxide and temperature rising and falling together through successive ice ages, a pattern that has become one of the strongest pieces of evidence for the link between the two.
By drilling cores from the thickest ice sheets and analyzing the air in successive layers, scientists have reconstructed carbon dioxide levels stretching back hundreds of thousands of years.
The method has a subtlety that is easy to overlook.
The trapped air is therefore younger than the ice around it, sometimes by thousands of years.
questions.explanation: The final sentence states what the corrected records show and why it matters.

title: Museum labels
text: A museum label of fifty words can shape how visitors see an object more than any amount of scholarship in the catalogue. Studies of visitor behavior show that most people read labels, if they read anything, and spend only seconds doing so. Curators who write labels are therefore making some of their most influential choices in their briefest texts, deciding which single fact or interpretation a casual visitor will carry away.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that label writing is important chiefly because
choices: labels are often the only interpretation most visitors read
catalogues are poorly written
visitors spend a long time reading labels
labels are more scholarly than catalogues
curators rarely write catalogues
questions.explanation: Most visitors read labels, if anything, and only briefly, so the label decides what they take away.
